sentences: In early September 1888, the doctor reads in the newspaper of the murder of the first victim in the poor district and alerts the detective, who takes up the case.
When the inspector visits the detective's lodgings to ask the detective not to interfere with the police investigation, the detective carries on regardless, visiting the poor district in disguise.

Over the following weeks the detective and the doctor examine the scenes of the murders of the second victim, the third victim and the fourth victim, gather witness statements and test their theories through reconstructions.

The detective concludes that the "taunting letter" is a hoax by the hoaxer, a journalist at the news agency hungry for a scoop, who coined the name "the killer's nickname" with the folklore figure the leaping phantom in mind.

By redrawing the street graffito in chalk and pouring water over it, he shows that the message could not have survived the night's rain unless it was written shortly before its discovery, and so was probably left by the killer.
Reviewing earlier attacks in the district, he rules out the assault on the earlier assault victim but attributes the killing of the earlier murder victim to the same man.

The detective eliminates a series of suspects, including the first suspect ("his nickname"), the street gambler the second suspect, the physician, the painter the fourth suspect, the widower the fifth suspect, and the sixth suspect, a Jewish former butcher who helps the investigation.

From the witness statements and his own deductions he profiles the killer as a poor, right-handed butcher aged about 33, roughly 5 ft tall with fair hair and moustache, who bears a grudge against the Jewish community, has a child suffering from syphilis, and lives in the neighbouring district.
After the murder of the fifth victim on 9 November, the detective reconstructs her mutilated body in clay at the detective's lodgings.
While looking for the witness the passer-by, he calls by mistake at a house in the market street, now the home of another butcher, the family man, whose wife and syphilitic son match his profile.
That evening the family man silently re-enacts his crimes in front of the detective.

The detective refuses to hand him over to the police headquarters: he says he serves the truth rather than justice, and he fears that exposing a Jewish killer would set off antisemitic violence in the poor district.
He asks the doctor not to write about the case and suggests he invent a story about a ghostly hound that glows in the dark instead, a nod to the famous novel.

The unnamed narrator opens with a lengthy commentary on the nature and practice of analytical reasoning, then describes the circumstances under which he first met the detective during a visit to the city.
The two share rooms in a dilapidated old mansion and allow no visitors, having cut off all contact with past acquaintances and venturing outside only at night.

One evening, the detective demonstrates his analytical prowess by deducing the narrator's thoughts about a particular stage actor, based on clues gathered from the narrator's previous words and actions.
The detective and the narrator read the newspaper accounts of a baffling double murder.
The mother and her daughter the young woman have been found dead at their home in the side street, a fictional street in the city.
The mother was found in a yard behind the house, with multiple broken bones and her throat so deeply cut that her head fell off when the body was moved.
The young woman was found strangled to death and stuffed upside down into a chimney, wedged so tightly that it took the strength of several men to pull her loose.
The murders occurred in a fourth-floor room that was locked from the inside; on the floor were found a bloody straight razor, bloody tufts of gray hair, and two bags of gold coins.
Several witnesses reported hearing two voices at the time of the murder, one male and French, but disagreed on the language spoken by the other.
The speech was unclear, and all witnesses claimed not to know the language the second voice was speaking.
A bank clerk named the clerk, who had delivered the gold coins to the ladies the day before, is arrested even though there is no other evidence linking him to the crime.
Remembering a service that the clerk once performed for him, the detective offers his assistance to "the police chief", the prefect of police.
Because none of the witnesses can agree on the language of the second voice, the detective concludes they were not hearing a human voice at all.
He and the narrator examine the house thoroughly; the detective dismisses the idea of the clerk's guilt and a robbery motive, citing the fact that the gold was not taken.
He points out that the murderer would have had to have superhuman strength to force the young woman's body up the chimney.
He formulates a method by which the murderer could have entered the room and killed both women, involving an agile climb up a lightning rod and a leap to a set of open window shutters.
Showing an unusual tuft of hair from the scene, the detective concludes that an "Ourang-Outang" (orangutan) killed the women.
He places an advertisement in the newspaper asking if anyone has lost such an animal, and a sailor arrives looking for it.
The sailor offers a reward, but the detective is interested only in learning the circumstances behind the two murders.
The sailor explains that he captured the orangutan while in the tropical island and brought it back to the city, intending to sell it, but had trouble keeping it under control.

When he saw the island orangutan attempting to shave its face with his straight razor, imitating his morning grooming, it fled into the streets and reached the side street, where it climbed up and into the house.

The orangutan seized the mother by the hair and was waving the razor, imitating a barber; when she screamed in fear, it flew into a rage, ripped her hair out, slashed her throat, and strangled the young woman.
The sailor climbed up the lightning rod in an attempt to catch the animal, and the two voices heard by witnesses belonged to it and him.
Fearing punishment by its master, the orangutan threw the mother's body out the window and stuffed the young woman into the chimney before fleeing.
The sailor sells the orangutan, the clerk is released from custody, and an embarrassed police chief sarcastically remarks that people should mind their own business.

The detective comments to the narrator that the police chief is "somewhat too cunning to be profound", but admires his ability "de nier ce qui est, et d'expliquer ce qui n'est pas" (a quote from the novel by the philosopher: "to deny that which is, and explain that which is not").
The unnamed narrator is with the famous local amateur detective the investigator.
The investigator when they are joined by the police chief, prefect of the city police.
The police chief brings to the investigator's attention the theft from the queen's royal boudoir of a letter addressed to her.
The thief is the unscrupulous minister, who switched the letter for one of no importance during a visit with the queen and who has since been using its contents to blackmail her.

The investigator agrees with two conclusions formed by the police chief: that the letter has not yet been made public, since doing so would lead to certain circumstances that have not yet occurred; and that the minister must have it close at hand, ready to disclose at a moment's notice.

The police have thoroughly searched the minister's home (referred to as a "hotel" in keeping with local word usage of the era) and person for the letter, including an exhaustive examination of the furniture, walls, and carpeting for any concealed hiding places, but have found nothing.
The investigator suggests that the police chief and his men repeat their search and requests a description of the letter, which the police chief provides.
A month later, the police still have nothing to show for their efforts and a frustrated police chief declares that he would pay 50,000 francs to anyone who can help find the letter.

The investigator tells the police chief to write him a check for that amount; once he has done so, the investigator produces the letter from a writing-desk and an overjoyed police chief races away to return it to the queen.

The investigator then explains to the narrator that the police did not take into account the psychology of their adversary in executing their search, drawing a parallel with a schoolboy he once knew who exploited his classmates' methods of thinking in order to win all their marbles at the game of odds and evens.

The police had assumed that since the letter was so politically sensitive, the minister would take great pains to conceal it; however, the investigator conjectured that it would instead be hidden in plain sight.
He contrived to visit the minister at his home, disguising his eyes behind green spectacles in order to covertly survey the rooms.
Hanging near the mantelpiece was a cheap card-rack with a dirty, half-torn letter in one of its slots.
The investigator determined that this was the missing letter, which the minister had folded inside-out, re-addressed and sealed, and damaged in order to hide its nature.
He left his snuffbox behind upon departing, as an excuse to return the next day.
Shortly after this second arrival, a disturbance occurred in the street outside, arranged in advance with a paid confederate.
While the minister was distracted, the investigator took the letter and replaced it with a duplicate he had prepared.
The investigator chose not to attempt to seize the letter openly for fear that the minister would have had him killed.

As he both supports the queen politically and bears an old grudge against the minister, he hopes that the minister will try to use the duplicate in his blackmail scheme and thus bring about his own downfall.

Instead of insulting the minister by leaving it blank, the investigator had written a quotation from the playwright's play the tragedy of the two brothers that implies he took the original: Un dessein si funeste, / S'il n'est digne du premier frère, est digne du second frère ("If such a sinister design is not worthy of the first brother, it is worthy of the second brother").
The author's detective character the investigator.
The investigator and his assistant, the unnamed narrator, undertake the unsolved murder of the young woman in the city.
The body of the young woman, a perfume shop employee, is found in the river, and the press takes a keen interest in the mystery.

In the story, the investigator explains that "it is the object of our newspapers rather to create a sensation—to make a point—than to further the cause of truth", and proceeds by exposing the contradictions in their theories.
Even so, he uses the newspaper reports to get into the mind of the murderer.
The investigator rejects the popular theory blaming the murder on a gang of ruffians seen in the area around the time of the young woman's disappearance.
One of such a group, he reasons, would have certainly confessed to the crime due to fear of betrayal rather than a bothered conscience.
Using the known facts in the case, the investigator further determines that a single murderer was involved.
This person was probably a sailor, and dragged the victim by the cloth belt around her waist at first, then switched to a cloth around her neck, before dumping the body off a boat into the river.
Finding the boat, the investigator suggests, will lead the police to the murderer.
An "editor's note" states that it would be inappropriate to relate details of what followed, but that the police did apprehend the true murderer with the help of the investigator's deductions.
The heiress, a young English woman, inherits a large Indian diamond on her eighteenth birthday.
It is a legacy from her uncle, a corrupt British army officer who served in the eastern country.
The diamond is of great religious significance and extremely valuable, and three Hindu priests have dedicated their lives to recovering it.
The story incorporates elements of the legendary origins of a famous diamond (or perhaps another famous diamond or a third famous diamond).
The heiress's eighteenth birthday is celebrated with a large party at which the guests include her cousin the young gentleman.
She wears the diamond on her dress that evening for all to see, including some Indian jugglers who have called at the house.
Later that night the diamond is stolen from the heiress's bedroom, and a period of turmoil, unhappiness, misunderstandings and ill luck ensues.
Told by a series of narratives from some of the main characters, the complex plot traces the subsequent efforts to explain the theft, identify the thief, trace the stone and recover it.
The first part Policemen on patrol in a dangerous area of the city hear a cry coming from the rough bar and go to investigate.
There is evidence of a struggle.
Two dead men are lying next to the fireplace, another is lying in the middle of the room.
A wounded man, who is certainly the murderer, stands in a doorway.
The chief officer, the inspector, tells him to give himself up, and he protests his innocence, claiming self-defence.
He tries to escape, and when he is caught he cries, "Lost…It is the Prussians who are coming."
The wounded third man blames the young rebel for leading him to this place, and vows revenge.
He dies shortly afterwards.
The chief officer, judging from the man's attire, concludes that he was a soldier, and the name and number of his regiment are written on the buttons of his great coat.
His young colleague, the detective, remarks that the man cannot be a soldier because his hair is too long.
The chief officer disagrees.

The inspector thinks that the case is straightforward – a pub brawl that ended in murder, whereas the detective thinks that there is more to the affair than meets the eye, and asks the inspector if he can stay behind to investigate further, and chooses an older officer, the old policeman, to stay with him.
The detective expounds his interpretation of the case to him, stating that the vagabond they had arrested is in fact an upper-class man.
He comments that the criminal's remark about the Prussians was an allusion to a famous battle, and reasons that he was waiting for accomplices.
He finds footprints in the snow outside the back exit to the bar, revealing the presence of two women, who were helped to escape by an accomplice.
An examination of the body of the supposed soldier leads to the discovery of a note, which reveals that his name was a common first name.
Nothing is found on the bodies of the other two men which gives a clue to their identities.
The judge, the baron's heir, arrives and commends the detective for the meticulousness of his investigation.
After a brief interview with the suspect, the judge leaves suddenly, apparently moved, leaving the detective to his own devices.
The suspect later tries to commit suicide in his cell.

The detective continues his investigations the next day, following leads on the two women, but when he goes to report to the baron's heir he discovers that he has broken his leg and will be replaced by M.
Under interrogation, the suspect maintains that he is an acrobat with an ordinary name, and that he only arrived in the city on Sunday.
He states that he went for a drink in the rough bar, was mistaken for a police informant, attacked, and defended himself with the revolver he was carrying.
After making further enquiries, including observing the prisoner from above his cell, fail to produce any information, the detective decides to take drastic measures.
The second judge to allow him to set a trap by letting the prisoner escape, so that he can follow him.
The acrobat wanders in the streets, followed by the detective and the old policeman in disguise, and eventually comes out of a seedy bar with a suspicious-looking man.
In the evening, they stop outside a town house, which belongs to the duke and the acrobat scales the wall, eluding his followers.
They arrest his accomplice and search the house and its grounds, but the suspect has vanished.
The detective goes to amateur detective, the old sleuth for advice.
The old sleuth states that the baron's heir's fall and the acrobat's attempted suicide were not a coincidence, and that the two are enemies.
By his reasoning it appears impossible for the acrobat to be the duke, therefore the acrobat and the duke are one and the same.
Through consultation of biographies of the duke and the baron's heir's fathers, he reveals the hatred that exists between the royalist duke's family and the Republican baron's family.
He says that the prisoner tried to kill himself because he thought his identity would be exposed and that this would bring shame on his family name.
The second part 1815.

The duke returns from exile to claim possession of his lands, the majority of which are now in the possession of the landholder, a bourgeois widower who live with his beautiful daughter, the young woman.
He claims that he had been charged with their guardianship until the return of the duke's family, but the Duke treats him like a servant and accuses him of profiting from them.

In their misfortune, one of their friends, the baron, under police surveillance as a former supporter of the former regime, asks the landholder for the young woman's hand in marriage for his son, the baron's heir, who is in love with and loved by her.
He refuses because he is planning an uprising against the duke's family, and does not want the baron's heir to get caught up in it.
The baron's heir becomes involved in the plans to be closer to the young woman, joining the landholder's son, the young rebel, and the farmer, who is secretly in love with the young woman.
Stopping at nothing that could help him succeed, the landholder is even welcoming to the duke's son, the marquis, who is enamoured with the young woman and hopes to make her his mistress.
As summarized in a film publication, the financier has plans for worldwide power through a mysterious secret that he possesses.
The gentleman burglar, master thief but loyal Frenchman, knows of the secret and is attempting to obtain state papers held by the financier.
Two other persons in the employ of the Kaiser are attempting the same thing.
The financier is murdered and some suspect the gentleman burglar, who announces his intention to catch the real killer.
Disguised as the chief of police, he works fearlessly alongside the police.
Soon he comes into contact with another master criminal, the impostor, who is masquerading as Maj.
A military man, and the gentleman burglar suspects that he is complicit in the crime.
The gentleman burglar falls in love with the lady, widow of the murdered man.

When the impostor, to get rid of the gentleman burglar, steals his daughter and informs the gentleman burglar that he will have to go alone to a deserted house to get her back, the gentleman burglar goes, foils the plot to kill him, and escapes through a tunnel that comes out in the home of the lady.
As he turns from the mantelpiece where he has discovered the hiding place of the state papers, he sees a mysterious man that he has been trailing.
To the gentleman burglar's horror he finds that the man is really the lady, who is in reality a German criminal.
She kills herself and the gentleman burglar escapes.
The rich man, owner of the famous emeralds, receives a letter stating that the emeralds will be stolen at midnight by "the masked criminal", and that police will not be able to stop the robbery.
The masked criminal, a figure dressed as a bat, murders the rich man and steals the emeralds.
The masked criminal leaves a bat-shaped note for the chief of police to inform him that he will be traveling to the country.
The masked criminal travels by car to a mansion built by the banker, the president of the local bank, who has recently been found dead in a distant state.
The mansion is being rented for the summer by writer the tenant, whose maid, the servant woman, sets up a bear trap to catch the masked criminal.
The young man, the banker's spendthrift nephew, wishes to lease the mansion, and plans with the physician.
The physician to frighten the tenant away.
The newspaper reports that the bank clerk, a cashier at the local bank, has robbed the bank of $200,000 and has disappeared.
The tenant's niece, the young lady, arrives with a supposed new gardener.
The tenant asks the gardener about his knowledge on alopecia, urticaria, and rubeola, and he answers as if the terms referred to plants rather than medical conditions.
On the staircase, the young man is shot, and the young lady manages to snatch part of a blueprint of the house from his pocket.
The first detective accuses her of trying to find a supposed hidden room in the mansion that should be shown on the blueprint.
The second detective arrives, and the group gets a call from the house phone in the garage, which sounds like groans of distress.
A circular light shines on the wall, with the shadow of a bat in its center, but after investigating, the group finds that the shape was caused by a miller moth on a car headlight.
The physician has the young lady recreate the young man's murder, and she notes that she tucked the blueprint in a bread roll on a tray, but the blueprint is now gone.

The new gardener is revealed to be the bank clerk, and the second detective attempts to arrest him for robbery, murder, and impersonation, but the young lady stops him, revealing that she and the bank clerk are engaged.
The physician searches for the hidden room by knocking on walls, which causes the others to investigate the sound, leading them to a ballroom which is supposedly haunted.

The candles in the ballroom go out when lit, and a shape appears to float towards the second detective and the servant woman, but it turns out to be the Japanese butler the manservant carrying a lamp.
After being confronted by the first detective, the physician knocks the first detective unconscious by striking his head, and he hides the first detective's body in another room.
A beaten man enters the house, and the second detective finds that he has no identification on his person.
The manservant sees a mysterious figure wearing a hat, and as he leaves to tell the others, the masked criminal's shadow passes by the door.
The masked criminal sets up a system of wires that attach to a light switch.
Outside, the bank clerk sees the figure in the hat crossing the roof, and realizes that it is the supposedly dead banker.
The young lady finds the hidden room, located behind a fireplace.
The masked criminal confronts her, demanding the combination to the safe in the hidden room, but she escapes.
The physician is accused of helping the masked criminal, and the masked criminal is soon captured and held at gunpoint.
However, the masked criminal activates the wire system, turning off the lights and allowing himself to escape.
The masked criminal flees outside but his leg is caught in the bear trap placed earlier by the servant woman.
The others find him and remove his mask, revealing him to be the first detective.

The beaten, unknown man announces that he is the true first detective, and that the man underneath the masked criminal's mask had stolen his papers, locked him in the garage, set it on fire and impersonated him.
In a decaying mansion overlooking a great river, millionaire the old man approaches death.
His greedy family descends upon him like "cats around a canary", causing him to become insane.
The old man orders that his last will and testament remain locked in a safe and go unread until the 20th anniversary of his death.
As the appointed time arrives, the old man's lawyer, the attorney, discovers that a second will mysteriously appeared in the safe.
The second will may only be opened if the terms of the first will are not fulfilled.
The caretaker of the family mansion, the housekeeper, blames the manifestation of the second will on the ghost of the old man, a notion that the astonished attorney quickly rejects.

As midnight approaches, the old man's relatives arrive at the mansion: nephews the first nephew, the second nephew, the timid nephew, his sister the aunt and her nieces the younger niece, and the heiress.
The old man's fortune is bequeathed to the most distant relative bearing the family name: the heiress.
The will, however, stipulates that to inherit the fortune, she must be judged sane by a doctor, the psychiatrist.
If she is deemed insane, the fortune is passed to the person named in the second will.
The fortune includes the family diamonds which her uncle hid years ago.
The heiress realizes that she is now like her uncle, "in a cage surrounded by cats."
While the family prepares for dinner, a guard barges in and announces that an escaped lunatic called the beast is either in the house or on the grounds.
The guard tells the younger niece, "He's a maniac who thinks he's a cat, and tears his victims like they were canaries!"
Meanwhile, the attorney suspects someone in the family might try to harm the heiress and decides to inform her of her successor.
Before he speaks the person's name, a hairy hand with long nails emerges from a secret passage in a bookshelf and pulls him in, terrifying the heiress.
When she explains what happened to the attorney, the family immediately concludes that she is insane.
Alone in her assigned room, the heiress examines a note slipped to her which reveals the location of the family jewels, fashioned into an elaborate necklace.
She follows the note's instructions and soon discovers the hiding place, in a secret panel above the fireplace.
She retires for the night, wearing the diamond-encrusted necklace.
While the heiress sleeps, the same mysterious hand emerges from the wall behind her bed and snatches the diamonds from her neck.
Once again, her sanity is questioned, but as the first nephew and the heiress search the room, they discover a hidden passage in the wall and in it the corpse of the attorney.
The housekeeper leaves to call the police, while the first nephew searches for the guard; the aunt runs away in hysterics and hitches a ride with a milkman.
The timid nephew and the heiress return to her room to search for the missing envelope, and discover that the attorney's body is missing.
The timid nephew vanishes as the secret passage closes behind him.
Wandering in the hidden passages, the timid nephew is attacked by the beast and left for dead.
He regains consciousness in time to rescue the heiress.
The police arrive and arrest the beast, who is actually the second nephew in disguise; the guard is his accomplice.
The second nephew is the person named in the second will; he had hoped to drive the heiress insane so that he could receive the inheritance.
After a sensational bank robbery, the ringleader of the gang, the master criminal—nicknamed the dreaded one—is still at large.
His old accomplices, the first accomplice and the second accomplice, have completed prison sentences, but the master criminal remains missing with a fortune in stolen gold.
The doctor, the proprietor of the old house—an eerie English abbey turned rest home—lives in fear.
Unknown to his guests, he is being blackmailed by a mysterious figure known as the blackmailer, whom he has promised his daughter the young woman in marriage.
The young woman is horrified by this unwanted engagement.
The old house becomes a gathering place for various odd guests.
Among them are the eccentric spiritualist the widow, the timid amateur criminologist the nervous guest, and the silent but observant butler the servant.
One night, a strange man known as the newcomer arrives, claiming his car broke down.
Though he appears drunk, the newcomer soon becomes entangled in the mystery.
Shortly after the newcomer's arrival, another mysterious guest, the lady guest arrives.
A series of increasingly strange and dangerous events proceed to unfold.
After the guests retire they report hearing ghostly organ music, though there is no organ in the house.
Next, the young woman is attacked by a mysterious figure in her own room.
The widow then proposes a séance hoping thereby to get to the bottom of the strange occurrences.
During the séance, while the lights are off, the blackmailer is struck on the head, and when the lights are turned on the lady guest is found to have been stabbed to death.
As the body is inspected it is revealed that the lady guest is actually a man to everyone's surprise!
He is eventually identified as the first accomplice.
The newcomer becomes a suspect to the murder when the young woman witnesses him picking up and concealing the murder weapon.
From this point, the young woman begins to doubt the newcomer, despite their growing attraction.
Eventually, the famed police headquarters detective the superintendent arrives.
He identifies the second accomplice, who had also turned up at the old house, and insists the real danger is still at large.
The newcomer, revealing himself to be an officer of the police headquarters, orchestrates a trap using the first accomplice's corpse as bait.
When the killer returns, the newcomer narrowly avoids being murdered and chases the figure—who abducts the young woman—into a secret chamber beneath the house.
In a climactic confrontation, the newcomer battles the masked assailant near a pit lined with knives.
Just as the newcomer is nearly pushed in, the superintendent and the others break through a panel and shoot the attacker, who falls to his death.
He is revealed to be the master criminal, alias the blackmailer, the dreaded one himself.
With the threat eliminated, the missing bank loot is recovered in the underground lair.

The doctor confesses he had been coerced by the master criminal, who had posed as his benefactor and manipulated him through threats and fear—including pressuring him into forcing the young woman's engagement.
The doctor admits he once attempted to kill the blackmailer to protect his daughter.
As the dust settles, the young woman and the newcomer (now revealed as a true police headquarters man) are seen beginning a romance, with the horrors of the old house behind them.
